subject: Accounting for sampling effort and spatial coverage bias in community HM

messages.author: 65b4deb3555c44c0
messages.subject: Accounting for sampling effort and spatial coverage bias in community HM
parts:
Hi everyone,
I am interested in using a community occupancy model with data augmentation (chapter 11.7 in Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology, Kéry and Royle 2015). I am opening this post because I have some doubts on how to deal with sampling effort and spatial coverage bias in the model, thanks in advance for any insight. 

My general idea is to use checklists from a citizen science project to estimate species richness (using data augmentation) within equal-area cells (10*10 km cells). Sampling effort and spatial coverage differ across cells: some 10*10 km cells contain multiple transects, some only one transect. Furthermore, transects differ in effort (time spent per 1 km of transect). I would like to account for these differences statistically in a HM framework, with the goal of understanding how the characteristics of different cells (e.g., % of urban land cover in the 10*10 km cell) relate to species richness. 

My case seems very similar to the analysis of Swiss birds presented in the book chapter "Inference About Species Richness and Community Structure Using Species-Specific Occupancy Models in the National Swiss Breeding Bird Survey MHB" in "Modeling Demographic Processes in Marked populations" (Kéry and Royle, 2009). It is also related to other articles, e.g., Royle et al. (2007) in Ecological Monographs (77(3)). Specifically, Kéry and Royle (2009) estimated species richness of birds in 1 km2 cells, where each cell was sampled with multiple transects at different sampling efforts. They used total transect length as a covariate in the state process (probability of species occurrence), and effort (time spent per transect/transect length) as a covariate in the observation process (probability of detecting a species). 

Why would route length affect the probability of occupancy of a species (rather than the probability of detecting a species)? Intuitively, species occur on a landscape independently of where we look for them. My initial idea was to model species richness as a function of covariates measured at the cell level (e.g., % of urban land cover in the 10*10 km cell), and incorporate in the observation process both transect length and effort, but reading these analyses indicates that this might not be a proper approach. I am wondering if there is a specific reason for using transect length as a covariate in the state process, if both approaches are valid, or if I am simply missing something.   

Any insight would be greatly appreciated, thank you very much for your time and consideration.
I hope that everyone is safe in these strange times.
Cheers,
Federico

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Accounting for sampling effort and spatial coverage bias in community HM
parts:
Dear Federico,

that's an interesting question and therefore I asked you to send it to the HMecology list.

I think that there are reasons for putting the spatial aspect of sampling intensity either in the occupancy model, as we did, or into the detection model, as you were thinking about doing.

Our motivation for putting transect length into the occupancy model was that all else equal, a species is more likely to occur in a larger than in a smaller area. So we viewed transect length as a proxy for the area covered within a 1km2 quadrat in the Swiss MHB. And then, we defined the ratio of total survey duration and transect length as a measure of sampling intensity, which would clearly not be expected to affect the true presence or absence of a species within the surveyed portion of the 1km2 quadrat, but rather only probability of detection.

However, a valid point can also be made for putting spatial effort into the detection model. This can perhaps be seen particularly well when you have a number of spatially distinct sampling sites within a 10x10km2 quadrat (although I think this argument would extend to the case of transect sampling as well). Such a design can be viewed as a multi-scale occupancy model, where you have your big 10x10 quadrats with multiple, nested sampling sites. These latter can be viewed as spatial replicates, and under certain assumptions you can estimate occupancy in the larger quadrat even without any further temporal replicates; see Sections 10.10 and 10.11 in the AHM1 book.

Actually, I would think about your case exactly in terms of such a multi-scale occupancy model, where you can estimate large-scale occupancy at the scale of the 10x10km2 quadrat, small-scale occupancy at the scale of the transect, and then at the bottom level you estimate the usual detection probability based on replicated surveys within the same transects. There are different ways in which you can specify the relationship between large- and small-scale occupancy, and you can use such a model to up- or down-scale occupancy. See 2-3 really interesting papers by Petr Keil around 2012-2013.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.author: 65b4deb3555c44c0
messages.subject: Re: Accounting for sampling effort and spatial coverage bias in community HM
parts:
Dear Marc,
I discussed this with other colleagues and one HMecology user that contacted me in private, I'll share some insights that originated from these conversations. Thank you for your availability and suggestions. I highlighted comments from your previous answer in blue.

Our motivation for putting transect length into the occupancy model was that all else equal, a species is more likely to occur in a larger than in a smaller area. My understanding of the analysis presented in the book chapter (Kéry and Royle, 2009) is that it estimates species richness for equal-area units (1-km cells), using multiple visits of one transect conducted within each cell, in a one-year closure period. Therefore, samples differ in total sampled area but have the same "cell area". This is why I originally thought that transect length would have affected detection (p) rather than occupancy (psi). 

Let me make an example. Consider two 1-km cells have the same proportion of forest and elevation (the other covariates used to model psi in your case study), but differ in transect length. Why would psi differ between the two cells? The two cells have the same area and the same environmental conditions, so I would expect the model to predict the same probability of occurrence of a species (regardless of how long were the transects used to sample the 1-km cells; p, however, would be higher when sampling longer transects). Yet, the positive effect of transect length directly affects probability of occupancy. This remains to me counter-intuitive "ecologically speaking", but I might be missing something.

So we viewed transect length as a proxy for the area covered within a 1km2 quadrat in the Swiss MHB. And then, we defined the ratio of total survey duration and transect length as a measure of sampling intensity, which would clearly not be expected to affect the true presence or absence of a species within the surveyed portion of the 1km2 quadrat, but rather only probability of detection.

Adding on my previous comment, if we are estimating occurrence (and subsequently richness) at the cell level, then I see transect length and total surveying time as two dimensions of heterogeneity in effort - "spatial" and "temporal" effort.

However, a valid point can also be made for putting spatial effort into the detection model. This can perhaps be seen particularly well when you have a number of spatially distinct sampling sites within a 10x10km2 quadrat (although I think this argument would extend to the case of transect sampling as well). Such a design can be viewed as a multi-scale occupancy model, where you have your big 10x10 quadrats with multiple, nested sampling sites. These latter can be viewed as spatial replicates, and under certain assumptions you can estimate occupancy in the larger quadrat even without any further temporal replicates; see Sections 10.10 and 10.11 in the AHM1 book. Actually, I would think about your case exactly in terms of such a multi-scale occupancy model, where you can estimate large-scale occupancy at the scale of the 10x10km2 quadrat, small-scale occupancy at the scale of the transect, and then at the bottom level you estimate the usual detection probability based on replicated surveys within the same transects. There are different ways in which you can specify the relationship between large- and small-scale occupancy, and you can use such a model to up- or down-scale occupancy. See 2-3 really interesting papers by Petr Keil around 2012-2013.

Thank you for this recommendation. I do have multiple transects within a landscapes, and a multi-scale approach seems definitely fitting. The focus of my study is estimating species richness at the "landscape" scale (a sort of "gamma diversity" of each cell, with each cell representing a landscape), and I found especially appealing the data augmentation approach. In principle, would it be possible to incorporate a multi-scale analysis with the data augmentation approach? I assume so, but please let me know if there is any mathematical/analytical limitation that makes this impossible. I really liked the series of downscaling papers from Keil et al. and how they applied it, e.g., to SAR, but my goal is to estimate species richness at the landscape (10*10 km cell level) based on a few 1-km2 cells within each landscape, rather than downscaling from the cell to each spatial sub-unit. I have read in the AHM book that the approach can go both ways, but I admit that I am still "digesting" it.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I truly appreciate your patience in talking about this. 
Kind regards,
Federico

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Accounting for sampling effort and spatial coverage bias in community HM
parts:
Dear Federico,

in the MHB the nominal sampling areas are 1km2 squares, but the effective sampling area of each quadrat is unknown, will usually be smaller than that and actually even depend on the species. We have a discussion of this in Chapter 6 of the AHM1 book. Formally, the inference in our analysis in that paper is *not* about the 1km2 areas, but about the unknown effective sampling area of each quadrat. Effective area can be assumed to be proportional to route length and this makes route length a sensible covariate for occupancy. I have some vague intuition that when you put route length on detection, then this implies equal effective sampling areas (which, if this was true, would actually be a good thing I admit). Some algebra would be great to clarify the issue, but I can't see how it would go right now.

About up-scaling: Perhaps the simplest in your case might be to formulate your model at the level of a cell associated with a transect and then use covariates and possibly spatial autocorrelation to estimate occurrence in the unsampled cells (i.e., where you have no transects). You can then estimate true presence/absence (z) for each species in every cell of the 10 x 10 km2 blocks and tally up presence/absence in the block as a function of the estimates values of z at the cell-level. You might not even have to formulate a multi-scale model for this. I once did such an analysis for 42,000 km2 in Switzerland, where I estimated parameters of the community model for about 125 species from about 2300 surveyed 1km2 cells (from a national Atlas project), then predicted occurrence for all 42,000 cells and tallied up species richness for 100 km2 blocks, which we call 'atlas squares'. Seemed to work OK, and can all be done based on the posterior samples of z so that you can even produce uncertainty estimates (e.g., 95% CRIs).

How well this will work in general will depend on several things though, including the proportion of the total area for which you have samples and also the configuration of these samples. And, be prepared for VERY long run times of your model or perhaps the need to implement it in other software such as Nimble or Stan.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Accounting for sampling effort and spatial coverage bias in community HM
parts:
Dear Federico,

I wouldn't say you were confused, b/c we may have been unclear about the exact interpretation of space in our analyses. The thing is that we, and everybody else, always say that our survey unit has such and such nominal area, in our case 1km2. But: the effective sampling area is unknown (and will vary as a function of (in our case) transect length and configuration), unless you use distance sampling or spatial capture-recapture. Putting route length on occupancy is an attempt to correct for variability in occupancy due to varying effective sampling area, but, again, a point could be made to put it instead into the detection model.

I must do a Nimble project soon to get into that software more. Start should be easy, since the model definition syntax is about 90% or more the same as in JAGS.

AHM2 should be available on Amazon.

Good luck and best regards  --- Marc
